lead: A filter, an attenuator pad, a length of transmission line — each is a two-port, and a large network is often built by wiring small two-ports together. Three connections cover almost every case. In series the port voltages add, so the Z matrices add. In parallel the port currents add, so the Y matrices add. In cascade the output of one two-port feeds the input of the next, so the ABCD matrices multiply. Each rule is a shortcut that saves you from solving the whole network from scratch, and the series and parallel rules each carry a port condition that must be checked first.
prereq: You need: 6.2 for Z and Y parameters, 6.4 for ABCD parameters, and 6.5 for converting between them.

blocks.text: Join port 1 of network A in series with port 1 of network B, and port 2 of A in series with port 2 of B. This is a series–series connection. The two networks sit back to back, so the current entering the pair at port 1 must pass through both of them.

The port currents are therefore shared: I1 flows through A and through B, and I2 flows through both on the output side. The port voltages split: V1 = V1a + V1b and V2 = V2a + V2b. Each network obeys V = ZI, so adding the two voltage equations gives the combined matrix.

blocks.where: Z, Z1, Z2 are 2×2 impedance matrices in ohms, Z1 for the first network and Z2 for the second; the addition is element by element, so z11 = z11a + z11b, z12 = z12a + z12b, z21 = z21a + z21b, z22 = z22a + z22b.

blocks.text: Port condition. The rule holds only if no current circulates between the two networks at the junctions. The only conducting paths between A and B must be the two port wires. If a third path exists — a common ground wire, a shared resistor — current loops through it, the port currents of A and B are no longer equal, and Z1 + Z2 is wrong.
Now connect port 1 of A across port 1 of B, and port 2 of A across port 2 of B. Both inputs see the same voltage V1 and both outputs see the same voltage V2. This is a parallel–parallel connection.
The port voltages are shared and the currents split: I1 = I1a + I1b and I2 = I2a + I2b. Each network obeys I = YV, so adding the two current equations gives the combined Y matrix.

blocks.where: Y, Y1, Y2 are 2×2 admittance matrices in siemens; the addition is element by element, exactly like the series case.

blocks.text: If your data is in Z form, do not add Z matrices for a parallel connection. Convert each network to Y using 6.5, add, and convert back only if the question asks for Z.

Port condition. Both networks must really see the same port voltage. If a circulating current can flow around the loop formed by the two input ports, or by the two output ports, then the currents you split into I1a and I1b are not the true branch currents and Y1 + Y2 fails. Check that the only connections are the two port pairs.

In cascade the output port of the first network becomes the input port of the second: V2a = V1b, and the current leaving port 2 of A equals the current entering port 1 of B, so I2a = −I1b with the usual sign convention. Filter chains and attenuator pads are built this way, stage after stage.

ABCD parameters are designed for this. With I2 defined as entering port 2 (the usual two-port convention), the chain matrix T satisfies [V1; I1] = T [V2; −I2]. The minus sign turns the entering current into the current drawn outward at port 2, which is what the next stage receives.

blocks.where: T is the ABCD matrix of the pair, T1 belongs to the network nearest the input, T2 to the network nearest the output, and × is ordinary 2×2 matrix multiplication, not element-by-element addition.

blocks.text: Order matters. With T1 = [[A1, B1], [C1, D1]] and T2 = [[A2, B2], [C2, D2]]: A = A1A2 + B1C2, B = A1B2 + B1D2, C = C1A2 + D1C2, D = C1B2 + D1D2. The input-side matrix sits on the left.

Cascade has no port condition. The output current of one network is the input current of the next by construction, so the product rule always holds for linear two-ports. Three or more stages multiply left to right.
Match the rule to the wiring, not to the matrix you happen to have in hand.

spec.title: Three interconnections, three rules
spec.aria: Three interconnections drawn one below another: series gives Z = Z1 + Z2, parallel gives Y = Y1 + Y2, and cascade gives T = T1 times T2.

examples.question: Two identical two-ports, each with z11 = 6 Ω, z12 = 4 Ω, z21 = 4 Ω and z22 = 7 Ω, are connected in series at both ports. The two networks touch only at the two port pairs. Find the Z matrix of the combined two-port and state whether it is reciprocal.
steps: The ports are in series at both ends, so the combined Z matrix is the sum of the two Z matrices: Z = Z1 + Z2.
Network A: z11a = 6 Ω, z12a = 4 Ω, z21a = 4 Ω, z22a = 7 Ω.
Network B is identical: z11b = 6 Ω, z12b = 4 Ω, z21b = 4 Ω, z22b = 7 Ω.
Port condition: the networks meet only at the two port pairs, so no circulating current flows and the addition is valid.
Check reciprocity: z12 = z21 = 8 Ω, so the combined two-port is reciprocal.
examples.answer: The combined Z matrix is Z = [[12, 8], [8, 14]] Ω, and the network is reciprocal.

traps: Cascade multiplies ABCD matrices; it never adds them. Adding T1 + T2 is the most common wrong answer in this chapter.
Do not add Z matrices for a parallel connection. Convert to Y first, add, then convert back if Z is asked for.
Matrix multiplication does not commute: the network nearest the source goes on the left of the ABCD product.
Z entries are in ohms and Y entries in siemens. Adding a Z matrix to a Y matrix, or dropping the unit in the final answer, loses marks.
Series and parallel both need their port condition checked. Cascade does not — do not claim a cascade is invalid because the networks share a node.

quiz.q: Which parameter matrix is added when two two-ports are connected in parallel at both ports?
quiz.a: The admittance matrices: Y = Y1 + Y2, in siemens.

quiz.q: Why do the port voltages add in a series connection?
quiz.a: The same port current passes through both networks, so the voltage across the pair is the drop across A plus the drop across B: V1 = V1a + V1b.

quiz.q: Two two-ports are in parallel, with Y1 = [[0.2, −0.05], [−0.05, 0.15]] S and Y2 = [[0.1, 0], [0, 0.1]] S. Find the combined Y matrix.
quiz.a: Add element by element: Y = [[0.3, −0.05], [−0.05, 0.25]] S.

quiz.q: Two identical two-ports with A = D = 2, B = 3 Ω, C = 1 S are cascaded. Find the ABCD matrix of the pair.
quiz.a: A = A₁A₂ + B₁C₂ = 2·2 + 3·1 = 7; B = A₁B₂ + B₁D₂ = 2·3 + 3·2 = 12 Ω; C = C₁A₂ + D₁C₂ = 1·2 + 2·1 = 4 S; D = C₁B₂ + D₁D₂ = 1·3 + 2·2 = 7. So T = [[7, 12 Ω], [4 S, 7]] and AD − BC = 49 − 48 = 1, as a reciprocal pair must.

quiz.q: A student connects two two-ports in series, but the two networks also share a common ground wire. Why is Z1 + Z2 wrong?
quiz.a: The ground wire gives a third conducting path, so a circulating current flows between the networks. The currents in A and B at each port are then unequal, which breaks the assumption behind the addition. Model the whole network directly instead.

quiz.q: For a cascade of two sections, T1T2 and T2T1 are different matrices. Which one is the combined matrix, and why?
quiz.a: T1T2, with T1 nearest the source. The input vector of the pair equals T1 times the output vector of the first section, and that output vector equals T2 times the final output vector. Reversing the order describes a different physical network.

beyond: Not for the exam. At microwave frequencies voltages and currents are hard to measure, so scattering (S) parameters replace Z, Y and ABCD; cascading S-parameters needs a scattering transfer matrix, not a plain product. Circuit simulators expand each subcircuit into the full set of element equations and solve the whole circuit at once by nodal analysis. The cascade rule is the hand-calculation shortcut you use when a chain of two-ports can be multiplied stage by stage; RF tools do the same thing with scattering transfer matrices. Power-system fault studies connect sequence networks in series or in parallel depending on the fault type, using the same two rules. Search 'S-parameter cascade scattering transfer matrix' or 'subcircuit expansion nodal analysis' to go further.
